title: US firms report early AI productivity gains alongside uneven adoption and job-mix reallocation
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34984 / Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Working Paper 2026-4, Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
geography: United States; corporate executives surveyed through Federal Reserve executive/CFO survey research

adoption.value: more than half of firms had already invested in AI, while many smaller firms were only beginning

productivity.value: labor-productivity gains were positive but varied across sectors, with the largest effects in high-skill services and finance
productivity.unit: reported executive assessment and firm evidence

expected_change.value: executives expected productivity gains to strengthen in 2026

observations.method: Survey of corporate executives combined with firm-level productivity and workforce analysis; the source distinguishes perceived productivity from revenue-based measured productivity.
observations.uncertainty: Executive reports and firm measures are not a randomized estimate of AI adoption; adoption selection, sector composition, measurement timing, and expectations can affect the comparison.
observations.subgroup: Firms of different sizes and sectors, especially high-skill services, finance, and smaller firms at earlier adoption stages.
observations.counterinterpretation: Early adoption and reported productivity gains may reflect firms that were already more capable or innovative; positive productivity does not establish worker benefit, consumer price reduction, or durable firm survival.

observations.period: 2026 survey; productivity measurement and revenue realization

denominator.unit: surveyed corporate executives and associated firm observations

capital_deepening.value: gains were not primarily driven by firms' capital deepening

revenue_tfp.value: gains were closely associated with increases in revenue-based total factor productivity and innovation- and demand-oriented channels

productivity_paradox.value: perceived productivity gains were larger than measured productivity gains, plausibly because revenue realization takes time

observations.method: Cross-sectional executive survey linked to firm productivity measures and interpretation of the timing gap between perceived performance and revenue realization.
observations.uncertainty: The productivity paradox is a measurement and timing interpretation, not proof that executive perceptions are wrong or that delayed revenue will materialize; the abstract does not provide every estimate or confidence interval.
observations.subgroup: Firms using rented or intangible AI capabilities, firms with innovation or demand channels, and firms whose revenue conversion may lag internal productivity change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Revenue-based productivity can miss quality, risk, consumer surplus, worker learning, and unpaid or unrecorded work; measured delay may also reflect weak demand or reporting differences rather than AI implementation lag.

observations.period: 2026 survey; near-term workforce expectations and job composition

aggregate_employment.value: little evidence of near-term aggregate employment declines due to AI

large_firm_expectation.value: larger companies anticipated AI-driven workforce reductions

small_firm_expectation.value: smaller companies expected modest workforce gains

job_mix.value: routine clerical roles declined in relative demand while skilled technical roles gained relative demand
job_mix.unit: reported within- and across-firm compositional reallocation

observations.method: Executive survey analysis of expected employment changes and job-function reallocation across firms and within firms.
observations.uncertainty: The result does not measure realized layoffs, hiring, wages, hours, worker voice, or household outcomes; expectations can differ from subsequent employment events, and job-function rankings do not identify individual transitions.
observations.subgroup: Large versus small firms, routine clerical workers, skilled technical workers, and workers in job functions ranked as more negatively affected by AI.
observations.counterinterpretation: A stable aggregate headcount can conceal displacement, upgrading, wage pressure, or reduced entry for particular workers; conversely, anticipated reductions need not occur if demand expands or implementation changes.

related_sources.claim: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta summary and working-paper link for the executive survey and firm productivity findings.
Federal Reserve paper version reporting the 734-executive sample and AI adoption, productivity, and labor-composition findings.

boundary: This record adds a US firm-level AI adoption and workforce-expectation layer to the industrial/consumer program. It does not establish a causal AI productivity effect, realized employment change, worker bargaining power, pay, consumer prices, firm survival, or household welfare; executive expectations and revenue-based productivity are not the same as worker or consumer benefit.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER W34984 page and linked Federal Reserve paper were reviewed for the 734-executive sample, uneven adoption, sector variation, productivity paradox, labor expectations, and job-composition findings.
